title: Caithness: 5 Haunted Places To Visit
excerpt: From ruined castles to abandoned kirks, Caithness is home to some of Scotland’s most chilling ghost stories and haunted locations.
content:
From ruined castles to abandoned kirks, Caithness is home to some of Scotland’s most chilling ghost stories and haunted locations

Caithness sits at the very top of mainland Scotland, where ruined castles face the North Sea and lonely kirks stand among windswept graveyards.

For centuries, this remote county has been shaped by Viking raids, clan feuds, shipwrecks and violent storms, leaving behind a landscape rich in history and folklore.

Unlike Scotland’s better-known haunted destinations, Caithness has no crowded ghost tours or queues of visitors. Instead, you’ll find dramatic castle ruins perched on sea cliffs, forgotten churches and quiet beaches where local legends have survived for generations.

If you enjoy exploring places where history and the supernatural seem to walk hand in hand, there are few better places to visit.

1. Castle Sinclair Girnigoe

Address: Sinclair’s Bay, Wick, Caithness KW1 4QT

Standing on a narrow headland above the crashing waves of Sinclair’s Bay, Castle Sinclair Girnigoe is one of Scotland’s most spectacular castle ruins. Once home to the powerful Earls of Caithness, it witnessed sieges, betrayals and family feuds that still colour its reputation today.

The castle is linked with shadowy figures seen moving through the ruins, strange voices carried on the wind and an overwhelming feeling of being watched in the old prison vaults. One of its darkest stories tells of Earl George Sinclair imprisoning his own son beneath the castle, where he was left to die after challenging his father’s authority.

Whether the ghosts are real or not, few places in Scotland combine dramatic scenery and grim history quite so effectively.

2. Ackergill Tower

Address: Ackergill, Wick, Caithness KW1 4RG

Just along the coast stands Ackergill Tower, a fortress whose best-known resident may be the Green Lady.

Legend identifies her as Helen Gunn, a young woman caught up in the bitter feud between the Gunn and Keith clans during the 15th century. Refusing to marry her captor, she is said to have thrown herself from the tower rather than surrender.

Today, guests and staff have reported seeing a woman dressed in green walking silently through the corridors before disappearing without trace. Others speak of unexplained footsteps, cold spots and an unmistakable feeling of sadness inside the building.

The tower’s commanding position overlooking the sea only adds to its haunting atmosphere.

3. Castle of Mey

Address: Mey, Thurso, Caithness KW14 8XH

Best known as the beloved Scottish home of Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother, the Castle of Mey has a quieter reputation that goes back much further.

Stories tell of another Green Lady whose spirit is said to wander the castle.

She is believed to have been a young woman separated from the man she loved, and visitors have reported hearing footsteps in empty rooms, doors closing by themselves and sudden drops in temperature.

Although beautifully restored, the castle has retained the atmosphere of an isolated Highland stronghold looking out across the Pentland Firth.

It remains one of Caithness’s finest historic buildings and is well worth a visit.

4. Olrig Kirk

Address: Olrig, near Thurso, Caithness KW12 6UN

Surrounded by open countryside, the ruined kirk at Olrig has long been associated with ghostly legends.

Local folklore tells of phantom pipers whose music drifts across the old graveyard on misty evenings despite nobody being there. Visitors have also described seeing shadowy figures among the gravestones and experiencing an uneasy silence that seems to settle over the site as daylight fades. Stories connecting the kirk with Viking spirits and sailors lost at sea have been passed down through generations.

It is a wonderfully atmospheric place that captures the lonely character of northern Scotland.

5. Keiss Castle

Address: Keiss, Wick, Caithness KW1 4XF

The ruins of Keiss Castle stand above the sea on one of Caithness’s most rugged stretches of coastline.

According to local legend, the castle is haunted by the Weeping Lady, a sorrowful figure seen standing in broken windows or looking out across the waves towards the horizon. Some believe she mourns a lost lover, while others connect her with one of the many tragedies that unfolded along this dangerous coastline. Sea mist rolling around the crumbling walls has only strengthened the castle’s eerie reputation.

Although nature is slowly reclaiming the ruins, Keiss remains one of the county’s most memorable historic landmarks.

Caithness rewards those prepared to venture beyond Scotland’s better-known tourist trails. Its castles, kirks and lonely coastline preserve centuries of history, while local ghost stories continue to give these remarkable places an added sense of mystery.

Whether you visit for the spectacular scenery, the rich history or the lingering legends, Caithness is one of Scotland’s finest destinations for anyone fascinated by the supernatural.
